name: Gastric bypass (Roux-en-Y)

card.summary: Major bariatric surgery that reroutes the gut for large, sustained weight loss, aimed at medical obesity rather than cosmetic leaning.
card.note: Major abdominal surgery with lifelong nutritional follow-up; guideline eligibility is based on BMI and health conditions, not appearance.

quick.overview:
Roux-en-Y gastric bypass divides the stomach into a small upper pouch and a large remnant, then reconnects the small intestine in a Y shape so food bypasses most of the stomach and the first part of the small intestine. It is one of the most studied bariatric operations.

It appears in looksmaxxing-adjacent discussion as a hardmaxx option for weight and facial leanness, but clinical guidance frames it as a treatment for severe obesity and obesity-related disease.
quick.mechanism: It was traditionally explained as restriction plus malabsorption. More recent work points to changes in gut hormones (reduced ghrelin; altered CCK, PYY, GLP-1), eating behavior and energy expenditure, though the mechanisms remain debated [1][2].
quick.risks: Complications reported include anastomotic leak, ulcers, strictures, dumping syndrome, bowel obstruction and internal hernia, blood clots, and nutritional deficiencies (iron, calcium, B12, thiamine and others). Eligibility under the 1991 NIH criteria is BMI of 40 or more, or 35 or more with comorbidities.

lead: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) is a bariatric operation in which the stomach is divided into a small upper pouch, typically about 15 to 30 mL, and a larger remnant; the small intestine is then rearranged into a Y so that food bypasses most of the stomach and the duodenum [1]. It is performed for severe obesity and its complications, and it is one of the best-studied weight-loss operations.

Large series report loss of roughly 65 to 80 percent of excess body weight, and Wikipedia reports improvement or resolution of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, sleep apnea and reflux in many patients [1]. A meta-analysis of the literature published in JAMA in 2004 examined weight loss, operative mortality and four comorbidities [2], and the Swedish Obese Subjects study reported lower overall mortality in the surgery group than in controls [3].

Clinical eligibility is set by weight and health status, not by appearance. In the looksmaxxing context the procedure is sometimes listed among hardmaxx options for dramatic weight change, which is a different use from the medical indication.

paras: The surgeon creates a small gastric pouch and connects it directly to a limb of small intestine (the Roux limb, typically 80 to 150 cm), so ingested food bypasses the remnant stomach and the duodenum. In the proximal version, the more common form in the United States, less intestine is bypassed; a distal version bypasses more and causes more malabsorption [1].
Laparoscopic RYGB was first performed in late 1993, and Rutledge developed the mini-gastric bypass in 1997 [1].

A 1991 NIH consensus panel set eligibility at a BMI of 40 or higher, or 35 or higher with at least one obesity-related comorbidity, and expects failed sustained weight loss through diet. A 2004 consensus conference of the American Society for Bariatric Surgery endorsed laparoscopic surgery and multidisciplinary preoperative evaluation [1]. Clinical guidelines for obesity care from the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and American College of Endocrinology also address surgical options [4].

The 2004 JAMA meta-analysis evaluated weight loss, operative mortality and obesity comorbidities including diabetes, hyperlipidemia, hypertension and sleep apnea, and concluded the operation generally led to improvement of these [2]. Randomized trials comparing bariatric surgery with intensive medical therapy in people with type 2 diabetes have reported greater glycemic control with surgery, including five-year results from a trial of RYGB and sleeve gastrectomy [5][6].

Wikipedia reports diabetes reversal in up to 90 percent of patients in some series, and a 2021 Lancet meta-analysis finding lower mortality after bariatric surgery in obese adults with and without diabetes [1]. The Swedish Obese Subjects study, a prospective controlled study of 4,047 people, compared surgery with conventional care for overall mortality [3].

Wikipedia gives 30-day complication rates of about 7 percent for laparoscopic and 14.5 percent for open surgery, with 30-day mortality of about 0.11 percent in US accredited-center data. Reported complications include anastomotic leak (about 2 percent), anastomotic ulcers (1 to 16 percent), strictures, dumping syndrome, internal hernia, bowel obstruction, bleeding and venous thromboembolism [1].

Nutritional deficiencies are common and can be under-recognized: calcium and iron (because the duodenum is bypassed), vitamin B12, thiamine, folate, zinc, fat-soluble vitamins and protein. Other reported effects include lower alcohol tolerance, post-operative depression and muscle weakness from reduced protein intake [1].

Weight loss was traditionally attributed to restriction and malabsorption. Later research points to hormonal and behavioral changes. A study in the New England Journal of Medicine compared plasma ghrelin after diet-induced weight loss and after gastric bypass [7], and work in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences examined gut microbiota in obesity and after bypass [8]. Gut hormones such as CCK, PYY and GLP-1 are involved, while ghrelin is reduced; the full mechanism is debated [1].

A 1995 report in Annals of Surgery described the operation as the most effective treatment for adult-onset diabetes mellitus, an early landmark in the metabolic-surgery literature [9]. Wikipedia places the first laparoscopic RYGB in late 1993 [1].

Human studies include randomized trials comparing bariatric surgery with intensive medical therapy for type 2 diabetes [5][6], large prospective controlled studies of mortality [3][10], and systematic reviews and meta-analyses of weight loss and comorbidities [2][11]. Registered trials include comparisons of banded and non-banded RYGB and of RYGB versus one-anastomosis gastric bypass [12][13]. These studies enroll patients with medical obesity; none was designed to test cosmetic or facial outcomes.

timeline.event: NIH consensus panel sets criteria for bariatric surgery: BMI 40 or higher, or 35 or higher with comorbidity [1].
First laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass performed [1].
Annals of Surgery report highlights diabetes remission after gastric bypass [9].
JAMA meta-analysis of bariatric surgery outcomes; ASBS consensus conference updates criteria [1][2].
Swedish Obese Subjects and a long-term gastric bypass mortality study report lower mortality after bariatric surgery [3][10].
